title: Best Time to Visit Pelling, Yuksom and South Sikkim
meta_description: Month by month in West and South Sikkim: Kanchenjunga view months, rhododendron season, monsoon landslides and festivals like Bumchu and Pang Lhabsol.
summary: October to mid-December is the best time for Kanchenjunga views from Pelling, Rinchenpong and Ravangla, with dry roads and cool, clear mornings. March and April bring rhododendrons at Barsey and good spring views. June to September is monsoon: green, cheap and quiet, but landslides can close roads and the mountain hides behind cloud.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: If the mountain is the reason you are coming, pick late October to mid-December. The monsoon has washed the haze out of the air, the sky is usually clear from dawn until mid-morning, and Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m, stands over Pelling close enough to count its ridges. If flowers matter more, come from mid-March to late April, when rhododendrons cover the Singalila ridge at Barsey and magnolias flower lower down.

West and South Sikkim sit lower than most people imagine. Pelling is about 2,150 m, Yuksom 1,780 m, Namchi 1,675 m and the Temi tea slopes lower still, so winters are cold rather than frozen. That makes this one of the better parts of the Himalaya for a winter trip.

sections.heading: Month by month
paras: This is how the year usually runs. Weather is never guaranteed in the hills, so treat it as a guide rather than a promise.

In short, the year splits into four seasons. October to December is dry and clear, the peak for views, treks and prices. January and February are cold, quiet and cheap, with good dawn views. March to May is spring, with flowers, tea picking and the busiest family holidays in May. June to September is the monsoon, green and wet, with the lowest prices and the most road trouble.

Holiday weeks matter as much as weather. The Durga Puja and Diwali weeks in October, Christmas to New Year, and the school holidays from mid-May to mid-June fill Pelling, and room prices can double. If your dates are flexible, the second half of November and the first half of December give peak-season skies at shoulder-season prices.

sections.heading: Clear-view months for Kanchenjunga
paras: The clearest skies come between October and December. On a good November morning the whole Kanchenjunga massif glows pink from Upper Pelling, the Sanga Choeling ridge, Rinchenpong, Hee Bermiok and the Ravangla road. January and February are often clear too, but the light is harsher and afternoons can cloud over. In March and April the dawn view is usually there, but dust and haze close in by 10 am.
From May the clouds sit on the range for days at a time. You may still get a break at dawn after a night of rain, which is why local photographers keep checking from 5 am even in June.

Altitude helps. Sanga Choeling and the ridge above Upper Pelling sit high enough to look over the morning mist that fills the Rangeet valley, while Rinchenpong and Hee Bermiok face the range directly across the valley. Ravangla gives a wider view along the Kanchenjunga massif and towards the peaks of North Sikkim on clear winter days.
list: Be outside 15 minutes before sunrise; the first light is the clearest.
Stay two nights or more in one view village so you get two chances.
Choose a room facing north-west in Pelling, or ask your homestay where the view is.

sections.heading: Rhododendrons and spring
paras: Sikkim has dozens of rhododendron species, and Rhododendron niveum is the state tree. The best place to see them is Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary on the Singalila ridge, where the 4 km walk from Hilley passes through forest in red, pink and white from mid-March to early May. Lower slopes bloom first; the higher forest around Barsey peaks in April. On the Goecha La trail the blooms above Tshoka and Dzongri come later, in late April and May.

Spring is also when Temi Tea Garden picks its first flush, in March and April, and when the Goecha La trekking season reopens. Days are pleasant at 15–20°C in Pelling, with occasional hail showers in the afternoon.

Ravangla's Maenam Hill, about 3,200 m, has its own rhododendron forest on the walk up through Maenam Wildlife Sanctuary, at its best in April. Around Pelling and Rinchenpong, look for magnolias in March and early April, before most of the rhododendrons at height have opened.

sections.heading: Monsoon and landslides
paras: The monsoon usually reaches Sikkim in early to mid June and lasts into September. West and South Sikkim get heavy rain, and the roads from Siliguri along the Teesta to Melli and on to Jorethang, and from Jorethang up to Pelling and Yuksom, can be blocked by landslides for hours or days. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood, parts of NH10 have had long closures and diversions. Check current status before you travel, and leave a spare day at the end of the trip.

The upside is real: green terraces, roaring falls at Rimbi and Kanchenjunga Falls, empty monasteries and hotel discounts of 30–50 percent. Leeches come out on forest paths, so wear closed shoes and carry salt. Treks to Dzongri and Goecha La are usually not run in July and August.

sections.heading: Festivals worth planning around
paras: Most festivals here follow the Tibetan lunar calendar, so dates move by a few weeks each year. Confirm each year's dates locally and check current status before you travel.

Festival days are a good reason to come, but also a reason to book early. Rooms in Yuksom and Legship fill around Bumchu, and Ravangla is busy over Pang Lhabsol. Stay in a nearby village homestay if the town is full; shared jeeps run in from the surrounding villages on the main day.
list: Bumchu at Tashiding, 14th–15th day of the first Tibetan month (February or March): the sacred vase is opened and its water read as a forecast for the year.
Pemayangtse cham, the masked dances held in February or March before Losar, in the monastery courtyard near Pelling.
Pang Lhabsol, 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month (August or September): Kanchenjunga is honoured as guardian deity, with warrior dances; Ravangla hosts a large celebration.
Tendong Lho Rum Faat, 8 August: the Lepcha festival giving thanks to Tendong Hill, which their legend says rose to save the people from a flood.
Maghe Sankranti in mid-January, with a large fair at Jorethang, and Losoong, the Sikkimese new year and harvest festival, in December.

sections.heading: What to pack for each season
list: October to December: down or fleece jacket, woollen cap, gloves for dawn viewpoints, sunscreen and sunglasses for the strong midday sun.
January and February: thermals, a warm sleeping layer, a hot-water bottle if you feel the cold, and lip balm for the dry air.
March to May: light layers, a fleece for evenings, a rain shell for afternoon showers, and a hat for walks to Barsey or Maenam.
June to September: a proper rain jacket, quick-dry clothes, closed shoes with grip, salt or leech socks for forest paths, and plastic bags for electronics.
All year: a refillable bottle, a small torch for early starts and power cuts, and any medicines you need, as pharmacies are limited outside Geyzing, Jorethang and Namchi.

sections.heading: Winter in West Sikkim
paras: December to February is underrated. Nights in Pelling drop close to freezing and snowfall in town is unusual, but skies are mostly clear, roads are dry and rooms are cheap outside Christmas week. Yuksom, Ravangla and Namchi are a little warmer. Pack a down jacket, a woollen cap and thermals, because few budget rooms have heating, and ask your homestay for an extra quilt. Barsey and the higher Singalila ridge can get snow, and the Goecha La trek is usually closed in deep winter.

Short days are the main cost of winter. Sunrise is around 6 am and dark falls soon after 5 pm, so plan to reach each night's stop by mid-afternoon. Shared jeeps run less often in the cold months, and some village homestays close for a few weeks around Losar or the family's own festivals, so call ahead.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit Pelling?
faqs.a: November is the best all-round month: dry roads, cold clear mornings and the best chance of a full Kanchenjunga view from Upper Pelling. Late October and early December are almost as good. For rhododendrons, come in late March or April instead, accepting some haze. Avoid July and August unless you want rain, low prices and few visitors.

faqs.q: When can you see Kanchenjunga clearly from Pelling?
faqs.a: The clearest views come from October to December, usually from dawn until mid-morning. January to April also gives dawn views, though haze builds through the day in spring. From May to September the range is usually under cloud, with occasional breaks after rain. Stay at least two nights to give yourself two sunrises.

faqs.q: Is it safe to visit West Sikkim in monsoon?
faqs.a: It is possible but needs flexibility. From June to September heavy rain can trigger landslides on the Teesta road to Melli and Jorethang and on the roads to Pelling and Yuksom, holding traffic for hours or days. Since the 2023 Teesta flood, NH10 has had long closures. Keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When do rhododendrons bloom at Barsey?
faqs.a: Rhododendrons in Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary bloom from about mid-March to early May, with April usually the peak around Barsey at 3,000 m. Lower slopes flower earlier and higher ones later. The timing shifts by a couple of weeks with each year's weather, so ask a homestay in Hilley, Okhrey or Sombaria before you set off.

Snow in Pelling town is uncommon, though it happens in some winters, usually for a day or two in January or February. Nights near freezing are normal from December to February. If snow is the goal, the higher Singalila ridge around Barsey and the Goecha La trail are more likely to have it, but trail access changes; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Bumchu festival at Tashiding?
faqs.a: Bumchu falls on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month, which usually lands in February or March. The lamas open the sacred vase and read its water level as a forecast for the year. Rooms in nearby Yuksom and Legship fill quickly, so book early and check current status before you travel, as the date moves each year.

faqs.q: What is the best time for the Goecha La trek?
faqs.a: April to May and October to November are the main seasons. Spring brings rhododendrons above Tshoka; autumn brings the clearest mountain views from Dzongri Top. Treks are usually not run in the July–August monsoon or in deep winter. Permits, route limits and fees change, and most groups now go only to View Point 1, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is December a good time to visit West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Yes, for those who can handle the cold. Skies are mostly clear, roads are dry and Kanchenjunga views are reliable. Nights in Pelling fall close to freezing and few budget rooms are heated, so bring warm layers. Christmas week is busy and pricier in Pelling; the first half of December is quieter and cheaper.

faqs.q: When is Pang Lhabsol celebrated in Ravangla?
faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol falls on the 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month, usually in late August or September. It honours Mount Kanchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity, with masked warrior dances, and Ravangla holds one of the largest celebrations. Dates move each year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
